security_spec.violation_condition: Kernel reads xtopei.IPRIO and assumes it equals the raw interrupt source priority iprio[i], then uses it for software-based priority arbitration or exposes it to a guest VM without accounting for: (1) saturation to 255 for iprio[i] > 255, and (2) priority=0 mapping to either 0 or 255 depending on whether the default priority is higher or lower than a machine external interrupt
security_spec.summary: If KVM or kernel interrupt handling reads xtopei.IPRIO and uses it as a raw priority value rather than a threshold-mapped value, major interrupts with iprio[i] > 255 all collapse to IPRIO=255, causing incorrect priority arbitration and potential guest VM privilege escalation through interrupt-priority injection

findings.finding: SW-file TOPEI emulation uses interrupt identity (i) as the PRIO field value (return (i << TOPEI_ID_SHIFT) | i), instead of deriving PRIO from per-interrupt priority registers (eiprio/iprio[i]). Real hardware returns a PRIO value that reflects programmed per-interrupt priority with spec-mandated clamping (iprio>255 → 255) and platform-defined priority-zero mapping. The SW-file does not model per-interrupt priority at all — the MRIF structure has no eiprio fields — so the PRIO value exposed to guests via VSTOPEI is the raw interrupt ID, not the actual configured priority.

VSTOPEI read path delegates to imsic_mrif_topei() when the VCPU uses the SW-file, returning a TOPEI value where the PRIO field equals the interrupt identity rather than the true per-interrupt iprio[i]. A guest VM that reads VSTOPEI and uses PRIO for software priority arbitration (e.g. nested virtualization, custom interrupt dispatch) receives incorrect priority values. The HW-accelerated VS-file path correctly reflects hardware priority semantics — this asymmetry creates a guest-observable side channel and reliability gap between SW-emulated and HW-accelerated modes.

extirq_update uses imsic_mrif_topei() as a pending-interrupt predicate but the threshold is used only as an ID-range bound (max_msi = eithreshold ? eithreshold : nr_msis), not as a priority threshold. If a guest configures per-interrupt priorities where lower-numbered IDs have lower priority than higher-numbered IDs, the SW-file will incorrectly report the lower-numbered ID as the highest-priority pending interrupt — violating AIA priority-ordering guarantees. No eiprio registers exist in the SW-file to track true per-interrupt priorities.

When reading state from HW VS-file into SW-file (clear=true during VCPU migration/release), only eip (pending) and eie (enable) bits are preserved. Per-interrupt priority values (eiprio) from the hardware are discarded — the SW-file has no fields to store them. This means that after a VCPU migration from one physical CPU to another, the guest loses its per-interrupt priority configuration if it subsequently runs in SW-file mode, silently corrupting the guest's view of interrupt priority ordering.

Host interrupt handler reads TOPEI via csr_swap() and extracts only the ID field (local_id >>= TOPEI_ID_SHIFT). The PRIO field is discarded. No guest VM is involved at this level — hardware does the priority-vs-threshold comparison internally. Compliant with spec.
Reads TOPI (not TOPEI) CSR and extracts only the IID field via topi >> TOPI_IID_SHIFT. TOPI.IID is invariant with respect to the iprio→IPRIO mapping issue. No priority values are exposed or compared.

Reads APLIC IDC CLAIMI register and extracts the ID field. The hardware IDC internally compares iprio-derived IPRIO values against the IDC threshold. The kernel does not perform any priority comparison or expose PRIO to guests at this level.

Guest IPRIO register RMW uses aia_get_iprio8/aia_set_iprio8 with TOPI_IPRIO_MASK (8-bit GENMASK(7,0)), correctly bounded to the 8-bit iprio register width. The IPRIO values stored/retrieved are the raw iprio[i] values as configured by the guest — the saturation/mapping is a hardware concern at the point where TOPEI.PRIO is computed from iprio[i], not at the iprio register level.

prio = aia_get_iprio8(vcpu, first_irq + i);
old_val |= (unsigned long)prio << (TOPI_IPRIO_BITS * i);
